cocos drops its frame and its wordmark — the mascot alone fills the envelope

L5 / prettier rider · cocos

Cocos publishes no vector (cocos.com serves CDN rasters; cocos/cocos-engine keeps editor/dashboard/logo.png), so the geometry is simple-icons' faithful vector of the mascot mark — the flame-headed character in a square frame with "COCOS" beneath it. Eighteen subpaths, and eleven of them go. The letters: each is 2.4–2.9×3.7 units on a 24-unit canvas, about 1.5 px tall at the fit with strokes a fraction of that. The frame: its rule is 0.40 px, and holding it in the fit costs the mascot the envelope — with the frame the whole mark runs 0.15 / 0.40 / 0.45 px, without it 0.40 / 0.95 / 1.55. That is tranche 1's casc reduction on the same reasoning (drop the field the reader cannot see, let the symbol fill the box). What is kept: the head, its outline and the two eyes; the six sub-pixel face details go. Both builds are in proofs/A02-t2-study.png.

36

RULE 2 in practice — one reused object glyph and seven brackets, three of them marks that exist

working rule 2 · command cobol codekit coloredpetrinets context controller denizenscript dinophp

Eight of the twenty-eight own no usable mark — 29%, against tranche 1's 18% and A01 tranche 2's 37%. command takes an OBJECT glyph and it is A01's, not a new one: a .command file is a shell script Finder runs in Terminal, which is the object .bat and .awk name, so it ships geom.terminalGlyph byte for byte across the slice boundary (Material draws the ⌘ key symbol, which reads the name rather than the file). Seven take the bracket glyph, and THREE of those are concepts whose mark exists: codekit and denizenscript publish theirs as raster only, which L2's fidelity rule ends, and dinophp publishes a real vector that fails L8's byte cap and L5 together (its own flag). The other four own no mark at all: cobol is a 1959 ISO standard (vscode-icons draws a triceratops, a joke about its age), coloredpetrinets is a formalism plus ISO/IEC 15909-2, context is ConTeXt — whose only mark is a logotype living in a FONT, tranche 1's cbx ruling exactly — and controller is an MVC file-naming convention. All seven payloads are byte-identical to A01's thirteen and tranche 1's four, and the slice check asserts that across the slice boundary.

37

the ambiguous names, and what the roster made them

L2 / roster reading · command controller context devenv cssmap cue cocos

Recorded because a wrong reading here would have put a real brand's mark on the wrong file type, and each of these was checked rather than assumed. command: .command with no language id is the macOS shell script Terminal runs on a double-click — not the ⌘ key, which is what Material draws. controller: .controller.js/.ts, icon-pack only, is the MVC controller layer of an Angular/Ngrx/Qwik app — a naming convention with no owner. context: .ctx with language id context is ConTeXt, the TeX macro package; Material added its icon in the "TeX/LaTeX related files" PR #3042, which is the corroboration. devenv: devenv.nix / devenv.lock / devenv.yaml is devenv.sh, the Nix developer-environment tool — NOT Visual Studio's devenv.exe. cssmap: .css.map is a CSS source map, so CSS's mark applies. cue: .cue with language id cue is the CUE configuration language, not a CD cue sheet. cocos: .prefab / .scene are Cocos Creator's scene files, so the engine's mark applies rather than a generic scene metaphor.

38

conan drops the JFrog frog its own lockup carries

L2 sourcing · conan

The mirror of tranche 1's chef flag, and it comes out the same way. Conan's own brand file — conan-io/conan .github/conan2-logo-for-dark.svg — is a lockup: the isometric Conan cube on the left, a divider rule, then the "CONAN 2.0 / C/C++ Package Manager" wordmark and the green JFROG FROG. JFrog owns Conan, and the company-mark rider covers a company standing in for a format IT owns — but Conan HAS its own mark, so the frog would be a parent company's symbol standing in for a product that does not need it, which is the Progress/Chef situation exactly. The cube ships; the frog, the rule and the wordmark are dropped. The flattening: the cube's two gradient faces take their offset-1 stop #21AFFF (7.65:1); the offset-0 stop #0086FD measures 5.16:1 and either would read, so the chrome default stands.

39

drools — Drools' own mark was built, rendered and declined on L5

L5 / prettier rider / working rule 2 · drools

The flag to argue with first. A .drl is a Drools rule file and Drools HAS a mark — the line-drawn face in profile, red contour, blue eye-line, orange tongue, purple brow — carried as a vector by gilbarbara/logos. It was fetched, built at the tall envelope and rasterised at a true 16 px, and it is declined on measurements rather than on taste. The numbers: its sustained ink runs are 0.50 / 0.55 / 0.55 / 0.75 px at the 5th, 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles, with 9.8% of the canvas inked — thinner at the median than the Buck 2 deer tranche 1 rejected (0.22 / 0.38 / 0.88). The eye-line is 0.94 px wide, the brow 2.11 × 0.75 px, and what arrives at 16 px is a red loop with three coloured specks in it (proofs/A02-t3-study.png). The prettier rider does not reach it: the rider reduces a mark's ELEMENT COUNT and thickens what is left, and here every element is a hairline, so thickening means redrawing the brand's own line weights end to end. The other mark this hunt found is not Drools': drools.org now serves the Apache KIE umbrella logo (its file is literally captioned "KIE Logo"), which is the mirror of the company-mark rider and the case tranche 1 declined for chef. To overturn: either rule that the KIE mark may stand for a .drl — one fetch, and it lands — or rule that a hairline mark may ship thickened, which reopens the deer and the dinosaur with it.

40

doctex / doctex-installer / dtx — the LaTeX Project's kingfisher, reduced to its silhouette

L2 / L5 / prettier rider / working rule 1 · doctex doctex-installer dtx

Three roster ids, one file family, one mark — and a reduction big enough to be worth arguing with. A .dtx is a literate LaTeX source, an .ins the docstrip installer that unpacks it, and the language id doctex names the same format, so all three take one mark and the family is declared. Which mark: LaTeX's recognisable mark is the "LaTeX" LOGOTYPE set in its own font, which R1 cannot ship (the ConTeXt case tranche 2 ruled on) — but the LaTeX PROJECT publishes real artwork at latex3/branding, the teal kingfisher that heads latex-project.org, and the company-mark rider ratified at the A01 gate says a format created and owned by a company may wear that company's mark. Same rider as cds/SAP one tranche back. The reduction, and both halves of it are forced: the bird is drawn with twenty-two WHITE FEATHER LINES over it, which measure 0.23–2.05 px at this envelope with eighteen of them under a pixel — and keeping them makes the icon 6,984 bytes against L8's 4 KB hard cap. Dropped, the icon is 1,739 bytes and the bird's own silhouette, jagged wing edge and all. Both builds are in proofs/A02-t3-study.png. Why this is not the editorconfig failure: that mascot's spectacles and features WERE the mark, so flattening destroyed it; these lines are feather texture inside a silhouette that still reads as a kingfisher at 16 px. To overturn: rule that an organisation's bird may not stand for a macro file and all three join the brackets — or that the flattening loses too much, which is the same outcome.

41

edge — the only SVG the brand publishes is a solid square

L2 sourcing / working rule 2 · edge

Worth reading because the hunt result sounds like a mistake and is not. An .edge is an Edge template (edgejs.dev, the engine AdonisJS ships — not Microsoft's browser, and Material's own icon for the id is "@", Edge's tag sigil). Its icon is a mint tile with a white frame and three white waves, and it is published as apple-touch-icon.png plus the android-chrome and favicon PNGs. The site's public/ tree does contain one SVG — safari-pinned-tab.svg — and that file is a potrace of a solid square: a single path whose only geometry is the 512 × 512 canvas outline. It is fetched and kept as sources-svg/edge-official-pinned.svg and rendered in proofs/A02-t3-study.png in the brand's own sampled #4CBBA5, so the claim can be checked rather than believed. vscode-icons draws a red serif "E" — a monogram in a colour the brand does not print. To overturn: rule that the PNG may be traced and the tile-and-waves ships.

42

dune — the brand's only image is a painting of a sand dune, and it ships

L2 sourcing · dune

The one call in this tranche that goes the other way, so it should be the easiest to disagree with. dune, dune-project and dune-workspace are the OCaml build system's files, and Dune publishes no mark at all: its only brand image is assets/imgs/dune_favicon.png, a PAINTED sand dune with a lit crest and a shadowed face, and ocaml/dune's repository carries no logo. A painted illustration has no vector geometry to recover, so a trace of it is an interpretation rather than a recovery — which is the argument for collapsing it. What ships instead is vscode-icons' four-layer flat reading of that same picture, and what justifies it is that BOTH source themes read the picture the same way (Material draws the same dune as an orange silhouette), which is the agreement L2's faithful-vector tier asks for. It renders well — runs 7.15 / 10.50 / 12.00 px, the thickest mark in the tranche. To overturn: rule that a picture is not a mark and dune joins the brackets, which is a one-line change.

43

eex and erb wear Elixir's and Ruby's own marks — and the family is FUTURE work

working rule 1 · eex erb

Two kin concepts with no base in the set yet, handled the way tranche 2 handled generated Dart. An .eex is an Embedded Elixir template and an .erb an Embedded Ruby one, so the marks that apply are Elixir's drop and Ruby's gem — and both brands publish them (elixir-lang.github.com's src/assets/icons/logo-elixir-light.svg, ruby-lang.org's images/header-ruby-logo.svg). Rule 1's branch (a) was checked for both: vscode-icons draws the Elixir drop itself for eex, and for erb it draws the gem as a dark-red OUTLINE — a recolour and a hollowing, which is the theme's own invention rather than a variant the brand draws (A01's al-dal reading). So both ship the base mark under their own id. No family is declared, because there is no elixir and no ruby subject in the pilot or in an approved slice to be byte-identical TO. What the next slice inherits: when elixir and ruby arrive, each has to be declared one family with its template id here — otherwise the twin audit will see two identical marks and fail them as undeclared twins, which is exactly what happened to al and dal inside this slice.

44

falcon — which Falcon, and an extension that matches none of them

L2 / roster · falcon

A name call, made from the artwork rather than from the roster, because the roster here is thin: it gives this concept the extension .falcon and the language id falcon, both from vscode-icons' icon pack, and no shipping Falcon writes .falcon files — the Python web framework's are .py, Falcon P/L's are .fal, and the marketplace's "Falcon Language" extension (vopple) registers .fl, .fle and .fles. What decides it is the mark vscode-icons draws for the id: a bird in flight, in oranges. The only Falcon that publishes a bird is the Python web framework, whose own falconframework.org/assets/logo.svg is the orange falcon with its wings spread and its talons down, and whose brand hex simple-icons records as #F0AD4E — the colour the drawing paints. So the framework's own vector ships. Two things to know: at 16 px it reads as "an orange bird" rather than as a falcon (runs 0.25 / 0.65 / 1.45 px), and at 4,070 bytes it is the largest icon in the slice, 26 bytes under L8's 4 KB hard cap. To overturn: rule that the id means Falcon P/L and it becomes a fresh hunt (that brand's mark is a stylised falcon head, published as raster).

45

elm — the geometry is the brand's vector, the COLOURS are sampled from its raster

L2 / L6 · elm

A first for this set, so it is flagged rather than buried in a simplification log. Elm publishes its tangram as a vector — seven <polygon> pieces in elm/foundation.elm-lang.org — but that file is the REVERSED cut: every piece is fill="white". The four-colour original sits beside it as assets/logo.png, a raster. Three third-party traces exist and all three disagree about the hexes (vscode-icons #5FB4CB/#EEA400/#596277/#8CD636, devicon #60B5CC/#EFA500/#34495E/#8DD737, Material its own palette). So the geometry comes from the brand's vector and each polygon's CENTROID was projected into the brand's own PNG and the pixel under it read: #60B5CC, #5A6378, #60B5CC, #7FD13B, #7FD13B, #F0AD00, #F0AD00 in document order, off a colour box that measures exactly 300 × 300 px. Why this is not the raster trace L2 bans: no geometry comes from the picture — the mark's shapes are the brand's own vector coordinates, and the raster answers one question the vector cannot ("what colour is this piece?"). To overturn: rule that a trace's palette is preferable to sampling and one of the three gets picked instead.

46

duckdb / emacs / ember — three round marks, and the look-alike lane

R8 / look-alike lane · duckdb emacs ember

The tranche's twin-audit finding, declared rather than hidden. Three of its marks are round because their brands draw them round: DuckDB's duck head, GNU Emacs's sphere, Ember's disc. emacs and ember are PLATE marks — an official field carrying a glyph — so the audit scores them against each other glyph to glyph (a white swirl against a white "e") and they pass. duckdb is not a plate: its yellow disc is the duck's HEAD and the dark shapes are its eye and beak, and declaring it a field to move it into that lane would be a misdeclaration made to satisfy a gate. Scored honestly, silhouette against silhouette, duckdb vs emacs is 0.940 and duckdb vs ember 0.986 on the 0.72 bar. Both pairs are therefore DECLARED look-alikes (the antlr / chrome instrument, opened at the A01 fix round): the audit prints their live scores every run and the separator is colour and interior — 173.6 degrees of hue against Emacs, 49.2 degrees and 27.1 points of saturation against Ember. To overturn: Ember's own brand kit publishes the same "e" as a ROUNDED SQUARE and as a plain square, both equally official, so ruling "no two full discs" costs one fetch and settles that pair; the emacs pair has no non-round cut on either side and would have to be ruled on as it stands.

47

ejs — the brand's own mark ships under L5's floor

L5 · ejs

EJS publishes its own vector (mde/ejs-site ejs.svg) and it ships whole, which means shipping under the floor: the crimson "eJS" letterforms measure 0.85 px at the 25th percentile and 1.00 at the median at the wide envelope, against L5's 1.2 px official-forced minimum. At 16 px the olive swoosh reads and the letters do not; at 22 the J and the S separate. The reason it ships anyway is that there is no thicker EJS to ship — these are the brand's own proportions, the prettier rider has no element count to reduce here, and tranche 2 shipped Cypress's 0.95 px ring on the same reading. To overturn: rule that a mark under the floor collapses and ejs joins the brackets.

48

elastic — the brand hex paints nothing, and the mark's bar is theme-negative

L2 / L6 · elastic

Two small things worth knowing before agreeing. The bar: Elastic's own component ships the Elasticsearch mark with its middle bar painted by the class euiIcon__fillNegative — black on a light ground, WHITE on a dark one. This set's ground is #121314, so the bar is white: that is the brand's own rule applied, not a colour we chose, and it is the same move tranche 2 made with Cypress's dark-mode favicon rules. The hex: the worklist and brand-colors.json both record elastic as #005571, and it stays the recorded primary even though no layer paints it — the mark is yellow, teal and white. #005571 measures 2.25:1 against the backdrop, which is exactly why Elastic does not use it in the icon either. The npm / git / dart precedent covers this (brand-colors wins the primary, the artwork's fills win the layers), and the folder pass is where it would actually paint something.

49

dlang — the brand's banner is cropped, on the file's own instruction

L2 · dlang

D's own images/dlogo.svg is a 481 × 89 STRIP — a width="100%" red rect with the white D and its two moons sitting in the right third — and its first comment line reads "This version is meant to be centered and cropped left/right as needed". So it is cropped: to the mark plus the banner's own top margin (10.44 units) on each side, which lands at 117.99 × 89, aspect 1.326 against the wide envelope's 1.353. The vertical extent is the banner's, untouched, and nothing else moves. It is flagged because a crop is still a choice: a different rule (crop to a square, crop tight to the mark) would give a different plate. To overturn: name the crop and it is one constant.

50

docz — the mark's line art is dropped, and it costs the ruled lines

L5 / L8 · docz

Docz's mark is a cream scroll with dark line art and a quill, published as a 1836 × 444 PNG on a CDN (docz.site itself is a parked domain now, serving a placeholder whose icon is an Arial "?" in a magnifier). vscode-icons' vector is that drawing layer for layer, and one of its five layers — the line art — is 3,972 characters, which on its own is more than L8's 4 KB hard cap allows a finished icon. It is also unfilled in the source, so it paints black: 1.13:1 against the backdrop. Dropped, on tranche 1's bruno reading. What it costs: the scroll's ruled lines and the quill's contour, so at 16 px the icon reads as "a document with a pen" rather than as Docz's scroll. To overturn: rule that the line art matters more than the cap and the layer has to be simplified subpath by subpath to fit — a real piece of work, but a possible one.

51

the collapse rate — ten of twenty-eight, and why this stretch of the alphabet

working rule 2 · docpad dotjs doxyfile drools dtd duc dustjs dylan edge

Worth stating at slice level rather than leaving to arithmetic: this tranche collapses nine concepts to the bracket glyph and one to a new object glyph — 36%, against tranche 1's 18% and tranche 2's 29%. It is not a change of standard. Six of the nine are concepts whose mark EXISTS and could not ship, each for its own recorded reason (drools on L5; doxyfile because the mark is a word; dotjs, duc, dylan and edge because the mark is raster only) — and the remaining three own no mark at all (docpad, a DTD has no owner to draw one, and dustjs). What clusters here is the long tail's dead projects (DocPad 2018, Dust 2019, ENSIME 2018, Open Dylan) and its file-format NOUNS — a Doxyfile, a DTD, a .dtx — which is what the D-and-E stretch of an extension roster is made of. If the rate looks wrong, the flags above are where to push: five of them are single rulings that would each move one to three ids back out of the collapse.

52

fix roundTHE RULING — a mark whose FIELD cannot clear the backdrop may ship the brand's own FRAME

guide §5 lift/plate erratum, amended / L5 contrast duty · cf cfc cfm

Recorded first because it is a law and not a subject. Flag 1 declined Adobe's ColdFusion plate on a measurement — its #002258 field is 1.21:1 against #121314, so at 16 px the plate is not there and two pale letters are left floating. Sebastian overturned it with a directive: "In those cases you can use a background in a frame with their corners rounded (like in previous iterations)", and, asked which frame, picked the brand's own — "Adobe's own framed icon — fetch Adobe's actual ColdFusion product icon: bright rounded frame + dark field + Cf letters, colors verbatim." What that binds, set-wide: where a brand publishes a FRAMED construction, a mark whose own field cannot clear the backdrop may ship it. The frame carries the silhouette; the dark field inside it is then mark-interior ink, which the §5 erratum already says is never lifted (dotenv's black on its yellow field is the same reading). So the trigger for a dark plate is no longer "lift it or drop it" — it is "does the brand draw a frame?" What it does NOT change: the frame has to be the BRAND's, derived from the brand's own artwork like any other geometry (L2), and it still has to clear L5 at 16 px — an invented keyline, or one too thin to see, is not a construction, it is a decoration. Scale: three subjects in this slice. cf, cfc and cfm are the only ones the trigger reaches; every other plate in A02 already clears the backdrop on its own field.

53

fix roundcf / cfc / cfm — Adobe's framed ColdFusion icon, and the one number the rider moved

L2 sourcing (ruled) / L8 / L5 prettier rider · cf cfc cfm

Provenance first, because the frame is Adobe's and not ours. Adobe publishes the ColdFusion mark twice and this build reads both, both fetched and both in the provenance pane. (1) coldfusion-official.svg, the 2021 logo, "Outline no shadow": a 56×54 #002258 rounded rect at rx/ry 9.9138 under a #7BADFF "Cf" in two paths — the plate, the corner radius, the letters and every colour. (2) coldfusion-framed-official.svg, Adobe's OWN framed ColdFusion product icon, fetched from adobe.com's product-icon directory and still carrying Adobe's internal filename cf_builder_2016_appicon.svg in its id: 256×249.6, a #CADBFE ring inset 10.7 around a #000F34 field. The frame constant, measured on four Adobe files rather than guessed: 10.7/256 = 4.18% here, and exactly 10/240 = w/24 on FrameMaker and RoboHelp, the two siblings Adobe serves from the same directory in the same generation, and on Adobe's rounded framed cut as well. The corners. Adobe's framed ColdFusion is SQUARE-cornered and the ruling asked for rounded, so the rounding comes from Adobe too: photoshop-ipad-official.svg is a 240×234 outer rect at r 42.5 around a 220×214 field at r 36.3, and 42.5/240 = 0.17708 is ColdFusion's own plate radius (9.9138/56 = 0.17703) to five decimals — the same rounded rectangle at two scales. So the outer radius is ColdFusion's own and the ONLY number borrowed from a sibling is the inner ratio, 36.3/42.5 = 0.8541. The one thing that had to change, and it is the flag to argue with. Adobe's w/24 frame is 2.33 units on the 56-wide plate, which is 0.53 px at the shipped fit — five times under L5's 1.2 px official-forced floor, and rendered in proofs/coldfusion-frame-study.png it is a halo, not a frame. The prettier rider thickens the one element that carries the silhouette, and it is thickened inside Adobe's own way of specifying it: the frame stays a fraction of the plate width and the denominator moves 24 → 10, giving 5.6 units = 1.28 px. w/11 was measured first and lands at 1.16 px, under the floor, so w/10 is the SMALLEST legal departure from Adobe's proportion rather than a weight somebody liked. L8: the frame is a filled RING, never a stroke — an outer contour with an inner one wound against it, punched by plain nonzero fill, which is how Adobe draws it too (it declares fill-rule:evenodd; this set emits none, so the winding does the work). A01's vsix flag records what happens when two subpaths are wound the same way and the counter never opens; that was checked for here. What it costs at 16 px: the frame reads and the letters are marginal — the "Cf" is 7.10×6.18 px at sustained ink runs of 0.97 / 1.06 / 1.19 px, so it arrives as an open arc beside a crossed stem rather than as crisp letterforms. That is Adobe's own drawing at this size, and thickening it would be redrawing a brand's letterforms, which L2 hard-rejects. To overturn: say the frame should be heavier and the denominator moves again — the study renders w/24, w/11 and w/10 side by side so the trade is visible rather than argued.
